name: Shona
confidence_why: 9 independent first-hand descriptions agree (2 state the same rule, 6 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_quote: The accent generally falls on the next to last syllable before a pause.
sweep_summary: Shona is in the catalog as fixed penultimate, domain word and phrase together, on Stevick 1965:4 ('The accent generally falls on the next to last syllable before a pause'). Of the five title-hits, none is a first-hand word-stress description: Harford 1999 (Malilime 1) is a prosodic-minimality/OT paper with no online copy (medium priority, unclear relevance); Downing & Kadenge 2015 (SALALS, paywalled, abstract read) is about PStem vs PWord domains for minimality, tone and hiatus, abstract silent on accent (medium priority); the three Güldemann entries are one work on clause-level prosodic subordination — the 1997 ULPA monograph was downloaded open from the DNB/qucosa copy (saved with), and its sec. 4.2 (pp. 22-23) is a secondary survey that refines the classification: penultimate prominence is ordinative, its units are really syntagms/intonation units (phrase-level, i.e. word and phrase together), realised by length per Fivaz/Fortune (Doke denies length), with a Karanga caveat from Odden 1981:4 ('no stress was found on any vowel in Karanga'); the Herbert-volume chapter is paywalled at Köppe (low priority) and the 1993 thesis is superseded. Best first-hand statement read: Pongweni 1977:172-173 (held by the project), utterance-level penultimate lengthening crossing the word boundary (/ndawona: mbɣa/), confirming the catalog's classification; it does not displace Stevick but is a stronger co-citation. Also flagged: Downing & Kadenge 2020 (TLR, CC BY) could not be downloaded by automated download (publisher bot wall, the Internet Archive unreachable).

new_statements.quote: in Central Shona, the vowel forming the nucleus of the penultimate syllable in an utterance (I find this particularly true of declarative statements) is longer in duration than all the other vowels in the same utterance. ... Penultimate vowel lengthening means that in the sentence /ndawona j'umba/, "I have seen a lion" the vowel /u/ is marked for length:- /u:/. ... If, however, the word /Jumba/ were replaced by a monosyllabic word, the penultimate position would then be occupied by the last syllable of /ndawona/, "I have seen": e.g. /ndawona: mb^a/, "I have seen a dog". [scanned: j'/J = ʃ, ^ = ɣ]

new_statements.reading: First-hand statement by a native-speaker phonetician for Karanga/Central Shona: the prominence is penultimate vowel length, its domain is the utterance (before pause), and it crosses word boundaries (a final monosyllable throws the length onto the last syllable of the preceding word). This confirms the catalog's fixed penultimate, word and phrase together (phrase-level) coding with an explicit boundary-crossing example, which the Stevick 1965 deciding quote ('next to last syllable before a pause', re-read at many1258/ lines 1000-1036, p.4 Note 1, plus the -nyi enclitic case p.88 lines 6010-6027) states but does not exemplify. Güldemann 1997:23 (read this search of works with stress in the title) adds the caveat that Odden 1981:4 found no stress on any vowel in Karanga, whereas Pongweni (also Karanga) reports utterance-penultimate length; both agree there is no word-level lexical accent.

The secondary quotation agrees with the catalog's penultimate placement and refines the existing Pongweni-based statement by giving a word-level half-length on every phonological word in addition to the utterance-final full length; the transcription marks ˘ / > in the txt are extracted text renderings of Fortune's length diacritics.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every phonological word carries penultimate length (half-length), and the utterance-final word before pause carries a relatively longer penultimate length; two contrastive register tones exist alongside this 'ordinative' penultimate length.
new_statements.secondary_stress: not mentioned as such; the word-level half-length on non-final words functions like a subordinate prominence
new_statements.identity_note: Mudzingwa 2010 describes the Karanga and Zezuru dialects specifically; Pongweni 1977 (existing statement) is Karanga; Fortune 1980 is standard (Zezuru-based) Shona; Harford 1997 is general Shona with a Karanga aside. Fortune 1955, Carter & Kahari 1981 and Pongweni 1990 were not opened, so their dialect coverage is unverified.

new_statements.quote: Stress and lengthening. A Shona word at the end of a sentence, or before a pause, has the last but one syllable vowel lengthened and stressed: Vasvi:ka 'They have arrived'. The male speaker on the recordings shows variable lengthening, and there are some exceptions such as words that are shouted, e.g. Makorokotó! 'Congratulations!' and some greetings, where the final vowel is lengthened and stressed. This is shown as hyphen and vowel, e.g. makorokotó-o. [Book I, L.12 fn.:] From now on, heré is spelt in the standard orthography, without indication of the final lengthening. In the speech of some, the penultimate is lengthened

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement and domain as the catalog record (Stevick 1965: 'accent generally falls on the next to last syllable before a pause') and as Pongweni 1977 / Fortune 1980 held by the project (pre-pausal penultimate length); adds explicit exceptions (final lengthening+stress in shouted words, some greetings, and the tag heré) and notes speaker variability.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Prominence (vowel length plus stress) falls on the penultimate syllable of the word that stands sentence-final or before a pause; i.e. penultimate, assigned in the pre-pausal (phrase-level) domain, non-contrastive. Shona is otherwise described as a two-tone language (H/L).
new_statements.secondary_stress: none described; lengthening said to be variable in the male speaker's recordings.
new_statements.exceptions: Shouted words (Makorokotó-o 'Congratulations!') and some greetings have the FINAL vowel lengthened and stressed; the question tag heré has final lengthening for some speakers and penultimate lengthening (he:re) for others.
new_statements.identity_note: Carter & Kahari 1981 teach standard Shona with Zezuru-based recordings (they note one female voice has 'a slight Manyika accent'); the catalog record is for Shona generally (Stevick's FSI course); Pongweni's works describe Karanga (Central Shona); Fortune 1955 describes Central Shona (Zezuru-based standard).

sources.quote: Stress ist für ihn im Sinne von Hyman ein Mittel zur Prominierung einer Silbe je Einheit, in unserem Falle der Penultima. Diese Einheit ist das Wort, d.h. Akzent hat keine lexikalisch distinktive oder expressive, sondern ordinative Funktion. Wenn man die Einheiten (op.cit.:208) betrachtet, an denen Akzent als Grenzsignal fungiert und die Doke als words bezeichnet, wird klar, daß es sich eigentlich um Syntagmen handelt, welche sich durch den agglutinativen Charakter des Bantu zu Intonationseinheiten fügen. Daß die Prominierung der vorletzten Silbe, wie im Zulu, durch Vokallänge realisiert wird, verneint er. [Translation: For him (Doke 1931a:203ff) stress is, in Hyman's sense, a means of making one syllable per unit prominent, in our case the penult. That unit is the word, i.e. accent has no lexically distinctive or expressive but an ordinative function. If one looks at the units (op.cit.:208) at which accent acts as a boundary signal and which Doke calls words, it becomes clear that they are really syntagms, which through the agglutinative character of Bantu join into intonation units. sources.note: The melodic (grammatical) tone system of Karanga Shona verbs largely reduces to the addition of a H tone at the left or right edge of the stem, the edge depending on the stem's lexical tone; the melodic H interacts in complex ways with rightward H spreading, giving somewhat different surface patterns per inflectional category; choice of melodic pattern is almost entirely predictable from the word's morphosyntactic properties.
